en: Padminī Ratnarakṣita, Chapter 24.
Nagoya Takaoka CA 17: 39v4–10; input PDSz, 9.iii.2025, Kolozsvár.
Then, in order to answer the question, "How does the mantra become accomplished? he said:
"In response to the request, 'How does the accomplished mantra come to be?'"

**"Now,"** and so forth. **"Various bases of accomplishment"** means those which are the supports for various accomplishments; they are such because from them arises the fruit of various types of ritual actions (*karma*). **"Accompanied by service"** means through union with one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). **"Having taken up the *liṅga*"** refers to the *liṅga* of Mahādeva; some say it refers to one's own *liṅga*. In the mantras beginning with **"Oṃ Cāmuṇḍe..."**, the preliminary service (*pūrvassevā*) is likewise performed. In the mantra beginning with **"Oṃ Vajra..."**, it is also the same.
In all mantras where no specific [method] is mentioned, the preliminary service is likewise performed; such is the sequence of preliminary service.

"Then," and so forth. "The state of various accomplishments" (*siddhi*) means that one perfectly abides in various accomplishments; it is just as those results, which are of the nature of various activities, arise. "By ten thousand recitations of the service" (*sevā*) means by means of the yoga of one's own chosen deity.

Regarding the phrase "having taken the *liṅga*," this refers to the *liṅga* of the Great Deity; some say it refers to one's own *liṅga*. As for the mantras beginning with *oṃ cāmuṇḍe*, the preliminary service (*puraścaraṇa*) is exactly as described before.

Regarding the mantras such as *oṃ vajra* and so forth, it is likewise in all cases that for those mantras for which no specific preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) has been taught, the sequence of preliminary service is exactly as described above.

"Having stirred" (*āloḍya*) means "having written," as is the understood remainder. "Nāgapuṣpa" refers to the flower of the *nāgakesara*. "By the two *yakāras*" refers to the two wind-mandalas. "With upturned petals" means tossed upward by the wind-mandala. This is the meaning.

Having taken a leaf with its veins upturned, one should write on it with a crow-feather pen the syllable *ya* and within its interior the mantra: *hūṃ 3 amukaṃ uccāṭaya phaṭ 3*. Having written this on two leaves and joined them together, one should cast them into a river of wind-blown paddy or simply into a river. By reciting the mantra at night at a solitary linga, one causes the enemy to be driven away.

The term "mixed" (*bsres pa*) is a remainder [of the previous context]. "Nāga-flower" refers to the flower of the *nāga* tree. "By the syllables *yaṃ*" means by the wind mandalas. "Leaves stirred by the wind" means carried away by a whirlwind. The meaning is this: having taken leaves carried by the wind.

In that regard, having written on two leaves of birch bark with a pen made from a crow’s feather and ink made from poison and other substances the mantra: *hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ amuka-aucchatāya phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ*, one should join them together. At night, while reciting the mantra over a single *liṅga*, one should cast it into a whirlwind, a storm, or a swift river; thus the enemy will be expelled.

"*With fallen cow dung*," and so forth. Some maintain that the ritual applications (*prayoga*) beginning with "*Vāyavya*" pertain to this very mantra, as well as to the *Hṛdaya* and *Upahṛdaya* mantras of the Blessed One. Regarding "*In a temple*": [this refers to] a single *liṅga*. Regarding "*Of all*": the ellipsis is "all rites are accomplished through devotion to the Guru. The underlying sense is that there is no accomplishment of rites without the mantra received from the Guru's instruction.

Regarding the application beginning with "because the heavy [substance] has not fallen to the ground," this very mantra is also used. Some understand that the applications starting from "at the corner of the wind" refer to the Lord’s heart-mantra and near-heart-mantra. "Temple" (devakula) refers to the *liṅga* as one.
The phrase "of all" implies that [attainment] is accomplished through devotion to the guru above all else; the intention is that there is no accomplishment apart from the guru’s oral instructions.

"Two" refers to white and red; one should be counted as a single unit by means of these two. Likewise for *trikaṭuka* (the three pungents) and *triphalā* (the three myrobalans). "Of *puṣpadāru* and *haridrā*" means *puṣpadāru* and *haridrā*. "By the sun" means by sunlight. "By fasting" means by the *poṣadha* (observance day).

"Two" refers to white and red; both are to be counted as one. Likewise, there are the three pungent substances and the three fruits. "Flower-tree and coriander" refers to the flower-tree (*puṣpavṛkṣa*) and coriander (*ajājī*). "By the sun" means while traveling in the sun. "Observance" (*upoṣadha*) refers to the *poṣadha* fast.
Thus ends the commentary on the twenty-fourth chapter. [curl] ||
This is the explanation of the twenty-fourth chapter.
